query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In situ heating of sub-10 nm equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy nanoparticles under vacuum triggers kinetically controlled surface segregation of low surface energy elements (Au and Cu), leading to shape transformation and particle size reduction via evaporation, contrary to the expectation of high thermal stability from sluggish diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (sub-10 nm) in an FCC multi-twinned/icosahedral structure synthesized by pulsed laser deposition at 873 K on a silicon nitride membrane.
generation.intervention: In situ heating from 298 K to 973 K at a rate of 1 K/s under vacuum.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in vacuum with discrete heating steps at 473, 673, 773, 873, and 973 K, with analysis performed for up to 45 minutes at each temperature step to limit IR radiation interference on EDS measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface energy-driven active atomic diffusion leading to the segregation of Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface, which enhances local reshaping and facilitates evaporation of these elements.
generation.mechanism: As temperature increases (notably above ~673 K), the difference in surface energies causes Au and Cu atoms to diffuse from the nanoparticle core to the surface. This segregation promotes a change in morphology (from elliptical to spherical) and, in the smallest particles (2–4 nm), results in the loss of Au/Cu via melting or evaporation, thereby reducing the average particle size.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline expectation of high stability, nanoparticles will show a progressive loss of the smallest sizes (2–4 nm), a widened size distribution, reduction in average particle size due to the evaporation of Au and Cu, and a transition from elliptical (or multi-twinned/icosahedral) to more spherical shapes with increasing temperature.
generation.baseline: The theoretical expectation that high-entropy alloy nanoparticles should exhibit sluggish diffusion and maintain their initial size and structural fidelity to higher temperatures due to entropy stabilization.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to dominate in sub-10 nm nanoparticles and becomes significant above ~673 K, with variations possible based on particle shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedral) and size; nanoparticles outside the 2–4 nm range may display different kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative rates of Au and Cu self-diffusion and the exact onset temperature for significant evaporation are not fully constrained and may depend on subtle variations in nanoparticle geometry and local environment.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ STEM-EDS measurements during heating of the nanoparticles under the specified conditions while simultaneously performing atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. Track nanoparticle morphology, size distribution, and surface composition (especially Au and Cu concentration) at temperature steps (473, 673, 773, 873, and 973 K). Also, measure the self-diffusivity of Au atoms to correlate with the observed morphological changes.
measurements: Nanoparticle size and shape (morphology) changes via aberration-corrected STEM imaging.
Surface composition (Au and Cu concentrations) via STEM-EDS at each temperature step.
Self-diffusivity of Au atoms (and possibly Cu) as a function of temperature.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments do not show a significant enrichment of Au/Cu at the nanoparticle surfaces, corresponding shape transitions from elliptical to spherical, or reduction in particle size (specifically in the 2–4 nm range) above ~673 K relative to the baseline of minimal changes, then the hypothesis is rejected.
